To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the tensor product and CRT can be used to derive new convolution algorithms, that these algorithms have reduced operation count, that these algorithms are faster than the FFT, and that the FFT can be combined with the CRT to produce a faster algorithm.

(1) the CRT method is faster than the FFT for small to moderate convolution size, and the FFT is faster than the CRT for large convolutions; (2) the FFT is faster for small convolutions and the CRT is faster for large convolutions, and (3) the FFT and CRT methods can be combined for large convolutions to achieve faster run-time than either method used separately.
the tensor product and CRT are useful tools for deriving and analyzing convolution algorithms and that the combination of FFT and CRT methods leads to faster algorithms than either method alone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the automatic derivation and analysis of fast algorithms for computing convolutions.
the automatic derivation of convolution algorithms, and the automatic implementation of these algorithms.
the development of a new approach for deriving, analyzing, and implementing fast convolution algorithms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of the tensor product in conjunction with the CRT is the most efficient method of computing cyclic convolutions.
the CRT-based algorithms, in general, are faster than other methods for large convolutions, and the FFT-CRT method is the fastest for very large convolutions.
the CRT method is the best method for computing linear and circular convolutions for all sizes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CRT is a very effective technique that is useful for a variety of applications.

this thesis presents a new method for deriving fast convolution algorithms, a new algorithm for cyclic convolution, a new algorithm that is faster than the FFT for very large size convolations, a new algorithm based on the FFT for computing cyclic convolutions, and an algorithm for computing linear convolutions.
we have developed a framework for deriving, optimizing and implementing algorithms for computing linear convolutions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there exists a large space of algorithms for computing convolution, and that the best algorithm for a given problem can be automatically derived using symbolic tools and then implemented using automatic code generators.
the use of symbolic tools to derive, optimize and analyze algorithms can lead to the discovery of novel algorithms and methods that would otherwise not have been found.
there are a variety of fast convolution algorithms, each of which has a different window of performance and each has different advantages in different scenarios.
